claims.text: At high temperatures, differential thermal expansion between microstructurally distinct regions in HfNbTaTiZr produces localized residual stresses.
Localized residual stresses alter dislocation mobility in HfNbTaTiZr.
Residual stresses caused by thermal-expansion mismatch mediate the alloy's nonlinear thermoelastic response.
Residual stresses caused by thermal-expansion mismatch increase the alloy's creep behavior.
The as-cast HfNbTaTiZr starting material is homogeneous and has a uniform microstructure.
Applying transient thermal gradients induces localized thermal-expansion mismatch and residual stress.
Slight compositional or phase variations in HfNbTaTiZr have different thermal-expansion rates at elevated temperatures.
An inhomogeneous lattice response influences elastic modulus, creep rate, and overall stress–strain behavior.
Samples exposed to imposed thermal gradients will have larger lattice-strain variations than thermally equilibrated samples.
Samples exposed to imposed thermal gradients will exhibit greater elastic-modulus softening than thermally equilibrated samples.
Samples exposed to imposed thermal gradients will exhibit higher creep rates than thermally equilibrated samples.
Samples exposed to imposed thermal gradients will exhibit greater stress relaxation than thermally equilibrated samples.
Thermally equilibrated samples have lower creep rates and more predictable stress–strain responses.
Thermal-expansion-mismatch effects become pronounced above 600 °C and are especially apparent near 1250 °C.
Precipitate hardening and intrinsic dislocation dynamics may also contribute to the mechanical and elastic responses.

contradictions.description: The initial material is described as homogeneous with a uniform microstructure, while the proposed mediator requires microstructurally distinct regions with compositional or phase variations. The hypothesis does not explain how the required heterogeneity arises in the stated starting state.
